To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the [Cu2(µ-O)2] and [Fe2(µ-O2)] species, which are derived from O2 activation, can be used as catalysts for the functionalization of C–H bonds in enzymes and in synthetic models.

the DFT potential energies of the reaction coordinate are accurate and can be used to predict the kinetic parameters of the catalytic reaction, and the atomic-level mechanisms can be proposed based on the DFT potential surfaces.

the DFT potential surfaces of the [Cu2(µ-O2)] and [Fe2(µ-O)] cores, which are generated by the dioxygen activation, can be applied to reproduce the kinetic isotope effect and rate constant of C–H bond cleavage by high-valent Cu and non-heme Fe complexes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following: (a) the catalytic mechanisms of C–H oxidation, (b) the role of the Fe(IV) species, and (c) the role of [Cu2(µ-O2)] and [Fe2(µ-O)] cores in the catalytic cycle.
the development of a new methodology to predict the rate constants and KIES for the C–H activations catalyzed by transition metal complexes.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the [Cu2(µ-O2)], [Cu2(-O2)], and [Fe2(1, 1--O2)] cores are not involved in the catalytic C–H activation step.
the [Cu2(IV,II)(μ-O)2] species, the [Fe2(IV,IV)(μ-O) 2] species, and the Fe(IV) species are the active catalysts for C–H bond functionalization in the non-heme Cu and Fe enzymes.
C–H bond activation by high-valence non-heme metal complexes is a stepwise process, which proceeds via the formation of a C–H bond cleaved intermediate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the [M2O2]2+ (M = Cu, Fe) core is a good catalyst for C–H bond cleavage.
the [Cu2(µ-O)2] species is a good catalyst for the C–H bond cleavage of the C–H bonds in alkanes and arenes, while the [Fe2(µ-O2)] species is not a good catalyst.

the [Fe2(µ-O)2] and Fe(IV)-oxo species can activate C-H bonds with high efficiency, while the [Cu2(µ-O2)] species can only activate C-H bonds in the presence of a strong base, such as hydroxide or amine.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the catalytic mechanism is determined by the electronic properties of the metal center, which are controlled by the metal oxidation state.
the [Cu2(II, II)] and [Fe2(III, III)] species can activate C–H bonds by an electrophilic mechanism, and the Fe(IV) species can activate C-H bonds by a radical mechanism.
C–H activation is initiated by the nucleophilic attack of an oxygen atom on the C–H bond to form a metal–hydroperoxide species.
